description: Every row-filter operator the schema permits, applied to one shared record set. Exists because the corpus previously exercised only 9 of the 16 operators, so nothing forced the three SDKs to agree on the other 7 -- which is how a 9-vs-16 divergence shipped: a schema-valid 'between' policy crashed one SDK, silently dropped every row in another, and enforced correctly in the third.
notes: Expectations are derived from canonical-enforcement-spec.md section 7, not from any implementation. Every operator drops a row whose referenced field is ABSENT, including the negative ones -- that fail-closed rule is the point of the 'missing' record in each case. A field present with a null value is distinct from an absent field. An absent field is dropped by every operator; a present-null field is kept by the negative operators and matched by isNull, which is what keeps the pushed-down SQL form -- (col <> 'x' OR col IS NULL) -- equivalent to the post-fetch pass. Comparison operators treat a non-comparable value as a non-match rather than raising. 'like'/'notLike' use SQL LIKE wildcards and are case-SENSITIVE, unlike field-name and tag-value matching; 'matches' is a full-match regex. Each case carries a full policy rather than a bare filter so the shared corpus walk discovers it and validates it against policy-definition.schema.json -- a bare filter object would have been silently exempt from schema validation.

cases.name: notEquals-drops-absent-field-but-keeps-present-null
cases.notes: 'missing' is dropped because the field is ABSENT -- the negative operators failing open on an absent field was a real defect. 'nullish' is KEPT: the field is present with a null value, which is a different case. This is not an arbitrary choice -- when the filter is pushed into SQL the rewriter emits (col <> 'x' OR col IS NULL) precisely so the database and the post-fetch pass select the same rows. Verified against Postgres: the bare form keeps only 'mid', the IS NULL arm keeps 'mid' and 'nullish', matching this expectation.

cases.name: notIn-drops-absent-field-but-keeps-present-null
cases.notes: Same reasoning as notEquals: absent is dropped, present-and-null is kept, so the pushed-down and post-fetch paths agree.

cases.name: like-is-case-sensitive
cases.notes: 'ALICE JONES' is NOT matched. LIKE is case-sensitive in SQL, and a like filter may be pushed into a WHERE clause verbatim -- matching case-insensitively post-fetch would make the same policy select different rows depending on whether pushdown was enabled.

cases.name: notLike-drops-absent-field-but-keeps-present-null
cases.notes: 'ALICE JONES' survives because LIKE is case-sensitive, so it does not match the pattern. 'nullish' is KEPT and 'missing' is dropped, identically to notEquals and notIn: notLike is a negative operator, so the pushed-down form must carry the same (col NOT LIKE 'x' OR col IS NULL) arm. This case caught a real divergence -- Python dropped the null row while .NET kept it, and both rewriters omitted the IS NULL arm for notLike while emitting it for the other two negatives. Verified against Postgres: bare NOT LIKE keeps only mid and high; with the IS NULL arm it also keeps nullish.

cases.name: matches-anchors-the-whole-pattern
cases.notes: The pattern must compile as ^(?:alice|bob)$, not ^alice|bob$. Without the non-capturing group the anchors bind to one alternative each and 'alice smith' would match -- a real fail-open.

cases.name: isNull-matches-present-and-null-only
cases.notes: 'missing' is DROPPED, not matched. 'the field is absent' and 'the field is present and null' are different statements, and only the second is what isNull asks about. A carve-out would also be self-defeating: a projection that omitted the column would start satisfying an isNull filter, so narrowing a query could widen a result.

cases.name: between-is-inclusive
cases.notes: Both bounds are inclusive, and values are ordered [low, high].

cases.name: between-inverted-range-matches-nothing
cases.notes: An inverted range is not silently reordered. Reordering would enforce a policy the author did not write; matching nothing is the fail-closed reading of a range that cannot be satisfied.

cases.name: type-mismatch-is-a-non-match-not-an-error
cases.notes: Comparing a string to a number drops the row rather than raising. One malformed value must not abort the whole result pass.

cases.name: filters-are-ANDed
cases.notes: A row must satisfy every filter. 'high' passes the score filter but fails the region one.
